messages.author: e6530528db4b07eb
messages.subject: making genetic maps
parts:
Hi,

I am making genetic maps for mouse chromosomes. My input data set has 2398 individuals. For larger chromosomes, I have a few hundred markers. Chr 1 has 485. Two alleles only. It is taking a long time. Chr 1 has been running now for 9 hours and is still going.

Can I break up the chr into parts? Can I divide the data set into individual input files, say 100 markers or so each, and then just paste the output together afterward?

Henry

messages.author: 96353e7106735838
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] making genetic maps
parts:
I wouldn't recommend breaking up the chromosomes into pieces. I suppose that could work, but it shouldn't be necessary. If you do try to do that, you should use overlapping subsets of markers, to avoid edge effects.

What part of the analysis is taking a lot of time?
Can you give further details on the data and what you're doing?

karl

I have 2398 mice and at 60-400+ markers per chromosome.  I am using rqtl only to make genetic maps of each chr.  My mice are not F2 or BC's.  For mapping, I will be using something else.  But the genetic map will be done using rqtl.

The part that is taking a long time is estimating the map. I am using the following command:
mydata <- read.cross("csv", "", genotypes = c("12", "11", "22"), alleles =  c("1", "2"), estimate.map = TRUE, "chr1_align2_rqtl_input.csv").  I do see in the text that estimate.map=TRUE can be time consuming, and that est.map can be used later.  But using it later will still be time consuming.

Question:  In the paragraph on pg 26 in the book, where this is mentioned, you say that map positions can be included or excluded in the input data.  What are these positions?  cMs or bp?  I ask because the map to be estimated is the recombination distances between markers.  If cMs are included in the input, then there's no need to make the map.  It's already made.  Therefore, the positions must be bps.   Does including bp locations of markers help the program make the map?

messages.author: 96353e7106735838
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] making genetic maps
parts:
>
> On Tuesday, July 22, 2014 9:51:34 AM UTC-5, henry wallace wrote:
> I have 2398 mice and at 60-400+ markers per chromosome. I am using rqtl only to make genetic maps of each chr. My mice are not F2 or BC's. For mapping, I will be using something else. But the genetic map will be done using rqtl.
>
Estimation of the genetic map requires consideration of the exact cross design. R/qtl can deal only with specific types of designs: principally backcross, intercross, or recombinant inbred lines.

> The part that is taking a long time is estimating the map. I am using the following command:
> mydata <- read.cross("csv", "", genotypes = c("12", "11", "22"), alleles = c("1", "2"), estimate.map = TRUE, "chr1_align2_rqtl_input.csv"). I do see in the text that estimate.map=TRUE can be time consuming, and that est.map can be used later. But using it later will still be time consuming.

I would use estimate.map=FALSE, so that the data can be read in, and deal with the map estimation afterwards.

Generally, you want to first perform a number of diagnostics, in many cases omitting badly behaved markers, before you actually estimate the inter-marker distances.

> Question: In the paragraph on pg 26 in the book, where this is mentioned, you say that map positions can be included or excluded in the input data. What are these positions? cMs or bp? I ask because the map to be estimated is the recombination distances between markers. If cMs are included in the input, then there's no need to make the map. It's already made. Therefore, the positions must be bps. Does including bp locations of markers help the program make the map?
R/qtl wants cM positions not bp. But if you don't have prior estimates of cM positions, use Mbp positions or any sort of dummy coordinates that indicate the order of the markers along chromosomes.

On Jul 22, 2014, at 12:24 PM, henry wallace <henry.ee...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Also, I am combining data from two generations that are 10 generations apart. Most of the markers are used in both generations. But there are many generation specific markers. The newer generation tends to use more of these unique markers. So, I have lots of "NA"'s in my data, especially for the older generation. My plan is to use the recombination distances I obtain from rqtl and then impute across the NA's (haley-knott style). Just in case this is relevant to the issue of processing time...

Appreciable missing data does make it much harder to estimate the genetic map. But a bigger concern is the nature of the cross and whether R/qtl is appropriate for what you are trying to do.

karl

> > Question:  In the paragraph on pg 26 in the book, where this is mentioned, you say that map positions can be included or excluded in the input data.  What are these positions?  cMs or bp?  I ask because the map to be estimated is the recombination distances between markers.  If cMs are included in the input, then there's no need to make the map.  It's already made.  Therefore, the positions must be bps.   Does including bp locations of markers help the program make the map?  
>
> R/qtl wants cM positions not bp. But if you don't have prior estimates of cM positions, use Mbp positions or any sort of dummy coordinates that indicate the order of the markers along chromosomes.
>
>
> On Jul 22, 2014, at 12:24 PM, henry wallace <henry.ee...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> > Also, I am combining data from two generations that are 10 generations apart.  Most of the markers are used in both generations.  But there are many generation specific markers.  The newer generation tends to use more of these unique markers.  So, I have lots of "NA"'s in my data, especially for the older generation.  My plan is to use the recombination distances I obtain from rqtl and then impute across the NA's (haley-knott style).  Just in case this is relevant to the issue of processing time...
>
>
> Appreciable missing data does make it much harder to estimate the genetic map. But a bigger concern is the nature of the cross and whether R/qtl is appropriate for what you are trying to do.
>
> karl

messages.author: 96353e7106735838
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] making genetic maps
parts:
> oh....OK. Glad I asked you. Well, both my groups are relevant. I want to map phenotypes on the combined data from both generations. If I cannot simply pool them together and run in rqtl, then what could I do. Perhaps I can do the following...
>
> Can I estimate the map for the most recent generation (and do this by allowing rqtl to think it is an F2) and then assume those distances apply to the earlier generation at common markers? Then, as I was planning to do, impute at unique markers in either generation?

I would not apply the map distances estimated from one generation to the other generation, as the recombination frequencies are totally different.

Best would be to estimate the frequencies and then do the imputations, with the different generations separately, and then combine the imputed data for the QTL analysis.

> Also, when I make the map for just one of my generations, should I include parents and offspring? Or just offspring? When I do mapping, it will just be with the offspring. I was wondering if including parents in the making of the map helped improve the estimation of the intermarker distances?

You shouldn't include parents and offspring; each has it's own recombination frequency.

karl
